statement: A patient with symptoms of acute gastroenteritis is being evaluated. The physician must distinguish between Calicivirus and Reovirus infection. Which morphological or biochemical attribute is a definitive contrast between these two families?
options: Reoviruses have a segmented double-stranded RNA genome, whereas Caliciviruses have a nonsegmented single-stranded RNA genome.
Caliciviruses contain an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the virion, while Reoviruses do not.
Reoviruses replicate in the nucleus, whereas Caliciviruses replicate in the cytoplasm.
Caliciviruses are enveloped, whereas Reoviruses are nonenveloped.
Caliciviruses possess a DNA genome, whereas Reoviruses possess an RNA genome.
correctOption: Reoviruses have a segmented double-stranded RNA genome, whereas Caliciviruses have a nonsegmented single-stranded RNA genome.
optionExplanations: Correct. Reoviruses are unique among human RNA viruses for having a double-stranded, segmented genome. Caliciviruses are single-stranded and nonsegmented.
Actually, Reoviruses require a virion-associated polymerase to transcribe mRNA from dsRNA, whereas positive-strand Caliciviruses do not carry one.
Both virus families replicate in the cytoplasm, as is typical for most RNA viruses.
Both Caliciviruses (Norovirus) and Reoviruses (Rotavirus) are nonenveloped, allowing survival in the acidic gastrointestinal environment.
Both are RNA viruses; the difference lies in the strandedness and segmentation of their genomes.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 245 (Book Page): [Reoviruses] have 10 or 11 segments of double-stranded linear RNA... [Caliciviruses] have single-stranded, linear, nonsegmented, positive-polarity RNA.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of adenoviruses, papillomaviruses, polyomaviruses, poxviruses, herpesviruses, hepadnaviruses, picornaviruses, hepeviruses, caliciviruses, and reoviruses
statement: Poxviruses are unique among DNA viruses because they do not follow the standard anatomic pattern of replication. Which of the following is an accurate statement regarding their life cycle?
options: They acquire their envelope from the host cell nuclear membrane.
They utilize host cell DNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the nucleus.
They lack a virion-associated RNA polymerase.
They replicate entirely within the cytoplasm of the infected cell.
Their DNA genome integrates into the host cell mitochondria.
correctOption: They replicate entirely within the cytoplasm of the infected cell.
optionExplanations: Herpesviruses acquire their envelope from the nuclear membrane; Poxviruses assemble in the cytoplasm.
Poxviruses cannot use host RNA polymerase because that enzyme is sequestered in the nucleus; they replicate in the cytoplasm.
Poxviruses must carry a virion RNA polymerase to synthesize viral mRNA in the cytoplasm.
Poxviruses are the only DNA viruses that carry their own RNA polymerase in the virion, allowing them to replicate in the cytoplasm.
No human virus is known to integrate its genome specifically into host mitochondria.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 286 (Book Page): Note that all steps in replication occur in the cytoplasm, which is unusual for a DNA virus.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of adenoviruses, papillomaviruses, polyomaviruses, poxviruses, herpesviruses, hepadnaviruses, picornaviruses, hepeviruses, caliciviruses, and reoviruses
statement: A patient is evaluated for suspected acute hepatitis B infection. The laboratory findings show a negative result for HBsAg and HBsAb, but a positive result for IgM HBcAb. Which stage of the infection does this serological profile represent?
options: Primary infection with a mutated strain lacking the core antigen
Complete clinical recovery and lifelong immunity
The early incubation period before symptoms appear
The window phase during which HBsAg has cleared but HBsAb is not yet detectable
A chronic carrier state with low viral replication
correctOption: The window phase during which HBsAg has cleared but HBsAb is not yet detectable
optionExplanations: IgM HBcAb is positive, which contradicts the idea of a missing core antigen; HBcAg is highly stable and not typically mutated in this manner.
Recovery is characterized by a positive HBsAb test, which provides immunity.
During the incubation period, HBsAg would typically be positive, and IgM HBcAb would not yet have peaked.

The 'window phase' occurs when HBsAg levels fall below the limit of detection and HBsAb has not yet risen to detectable levels. In this gap, testing for IgM HBcAb is the only way to confirm a recent acute infection.
In a chronic carrier, HBsAg would be persistently positive for at least 6 months.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 332 (Book Page): Note that there is a period of several weeks when HBsAg has disappeared but HBsAb is not yet detectable. This is the window phase. At this time, the HBcAb is always positive and can be used to make the diagnosis.

options: Bullet-shaped particles, 75 nm x 180 nm
Brick-shaped particles, 250 nm x 400 nm
Spherical particles with a halo of spikes, 100 nm diameter
Thread-like filaments, 80 nm in diameter

optionExplanations: The bullet shape is the hallmark of Rhabdoviruses (e.g., Rabies virus).
The brick shape is characteristic of Poxviruses (e.g., Smallpox virus).
Spherical particles with a halo of spikes describe Coronaviruses.
Filoviruses are named for their 'thread-like' (filo) appearance; they are uniformly 80 nm wide but vary greatly in length.

statement: In comparing the diagnostic aspects of enteric viruses, which characteristic is specific to Rotavirus that distinguishes it from Norovirus?
options: Transmission via the fecal-oral route
Stability in the environment due to lack of an envelope
Ability to be detected by PCR-based assays
Presence of a segmented double-stranded RNA genome
Causation of watery, nonbloody diarrhea
correctOption: Presence of a segmented double-stranded RNA genome
optionExplanations: Both Rotavirus and Norovirus are primarily transmitted via the fecal-oral route, making this feature a commonality rather than a distinction.
Both viruses are non-enveloped (naked) and thus highly stable in environmental conditions, allowing survival outside the host.
PCR is the standard, highly sensitive diagnostic method for both viruses, and thus cannot be used to distinguish them biologically.
Rotavirus belongs to the Reovirus family and is unique for having a double-stranded RNA genome organized into 11 segments.
The clinical presentation of both viruses typically involves watery diarrhea without the presence of blood or inflammatory cells in the stool.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 321 (Book Page): Rotavirus has a segmented, double-stranded RNA genome surrounded by a double-layered icosahedral capsid without an envelope. The rotavirus genome has 11 segments.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of adenoviruses, papillomaviruses, polyomaviruses, poxviruses, herpesviruses, hepadnaviruses, picornaviruses, hepeviruses, caliciviruses, and reoviruses
statement: Which of the following DNA viruses is characterized by its ability to replicate within the host cell cytoplasm rather than the nucleus?
options: Adenoviruses
Hepadnaviruses
Papillomaviruses
Herpesviruses
Poxviruses
correctOption: Poxviruses
optionExplanations: Adenoviruses are non-enveloped DNA viruses that replicate in the nucleus using host RNA polymerase.
Hepadnaviruses, such as HBV, replicate in the nucleus where their partially double-stranded genome is converted to a covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA).
Papillomaviruses are non-enveloped, circular DNA viruses that replicate in the nucleus of squamous epithelial cells.
Herpesviruses are enveloped DNA viruses that replicate in the nucleus and acquire their envelope from the nuclear membrane.

Poxviruses are unique among DNA viruses because they replicate entirely in the cytoplasm. Because the host cell's DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is sequestered in the nucleus, poxviruses must carry their own polymerase within the virion to transcribe their genome.

statement: A 4-year-old child presents with a fever, conjunctivitis, and a cough. On examination, bright red lesions with a white central dot are observed on the buccal mucosa. This finding is considered pathognomonic for an infection by a virus with which of the following properties?
options: Double-stranded DNA genome with an envelope acquired from the nuclear membrane
Single-stranded DNA genome with an icosahedral nucleocapsid
Single-stranded, nonsegmented negative-polarity RNA with an envelope and helical nucleocapsid
Single-stranded, nonsegmented positive-polarity RNA with an icosahedral capsid
Single-stranded, segmented RNA with a segmented genome and negative polarity
correctOption: Single-stranded, nonsegmented negative-polarity RNA with an envelope and helical nucleocapsid
optionExplanations: This describes Herpesviruses, which form intranuclear inclusions but do not cause Koplik's spots.
This describes Parvovirus B19, which causes 'slapped cheek' syndrome, not Koplik's spots.
Correct. The clinical description (Koplik's spots) identifies Measles virus, which is a member of the Paramyxovirus family (negative-sense, nonsegmented RNA, enveloped, helical capsid).
This describes Picornaviruses or Togaviruses (like Rubella). Rubella causes a rash but not Koplik's spots.
This describes Orthomyxoviruses (Influenza), which cause respiratory symptoms but not Koplik's spots.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 312 (Book Page): Koplik’s spots appear several days before the rash and are virtually diagnostic. They are bright red lesions with a white, central dot that are located on the buccal mucosa... options: Enveloped, helical symmetry, single-stranded negative-polarity RNA
Enveloped, bullet-shaped symmetry, single-stranded negative-polarity RNA
Nonenveloped, icosahedral symmetry, single-stranded positive-polarity RNA
Enveloped, icosahedral symmetry, double-stranded segmented RNA
Nonenveloped, complex symmetry, double-stranded circular DNA
correctOption: Nonenveloped, icosahedral symmetry, single-stranded positive-polarity RNA
optionExplanations: This describes the paramyxovirus or orthomyxovirus families, which are enveloped and have negative-polarity RNA.
This describes the rhabdovirus family (e.g., rabies virus).
Picornaviruses are small, naked (nonenveloped) viruses with icosahedral symmetry and a positive-sense RNA genome.
This describes reoviruses, though they are nonenveloped. No common RNA virus with icosahedral symmetry and segmented dsRNA is enveloped.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: A new strain of Influenza A virus emerges in a human population that possesses a hemagglutinin subtype previously only seen in avian populations. Which genetic mechanism is primarily responsible for this major antigenic shift?
options: Phenotypic mixing with a Paramyxovirus
Point mutations in the RNA polymerase gene
Complementation by a helper DNA virus
Reassortment of genomic RNA segments
Intramolecular recombination of non-segmented RNA
correctOption: Reassortment of genomic RNA segments
optionExplanations: Phenotypic mixing changes the surface proteins of the immediate progeny but the underlying genome remains unchanged; thus, it doesn't create a new heritable strain.
Point mutations lead to antigenic drift, which results in minor changes, not the introduction of completely new subtypes (antigenc shift).
Complementation allows a defective virus to replicate but does not permanently change the genome of the progeny to create new subtypes.
Because the Influenza genome is segmented, coinfection of a single cell with two different strains (e.g., human and avian) allows for the exchange of whole segments, leading to antigenic shift.
Recombination is rare in RNA viruses and does not apply to segmented viruses like Influenza for major shifts; reassortment is the primary mechanism.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 238 (Book Page): Reassortment is the term used when viruses with segmented genomes, such as influenza virus, exchange segments... Reassortment of influenza virus RNA segments encoding the viral hemagglutinin and neuraminidase is involved in the major antigenic changes in the virus that are the basis for recurrent influenza epidemics.

statement: Which aspect of the Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) replication cycle makes it unique compared to most other DNA viruses?
options: The virus acquires its envelope by budding from the outer plasma membrane of the cell.
It produces progeny by binary fission within the mitochondrial matrix of hepatocytes.
Its genome is integrated into the host chromosome as an obligatory step for every cycle of replication.
It uses a reverse transcriptase to synthesize its DNA genome from an RNA template late in the cycle.
It replicates entirely in the cytoplasm using a virus-encoded RNA polymerase.
correctOption: It uses a reverse transcriptase to synthesize its DNA genome from an RNA template late in the cycle.
optionExplanations: Most enveloped viruses bud from the plasma membrane, but this is not unique to HBV and doesn't define its DNA replication strategy.
Viruses do not undergo binary fission; that is a characteristic of cells.
While integration can occur and is linked to cancer, it is not a requirement for standard HBV replication.
HBV is a DNA virus that uniquely employs a reverse transcriptase to copy full-length pregenomic RNA into the DNA genome for new virions.
Poxviruses replicate in the cytoplasm; HBV replicates in the nucleus (early) and cytoplasm (assembly).
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 229 (Book Page): [hepadnaviruses, such as hepatitis B virus (HBV), use RNA as the template to produce their DNA genome late in the replicative cycle.]

statement: Which virus is characterized as a nonenveloped agent with a single-stranded, positive-polarity RNA genome and is the leading cause of viral gastroenteritis outbreaks on cruise ships?

Poliovirus
Rotavirus
Adenovirus type 40
Norovirus

optionExplanations: Hepatitis E (Hepevirus) causes hepatitis, not gastroenteritis, though it is also nonenveloped and positive-sense RNA.
Poliovirus is a picornavirus that causes paralysis or meningitis, not outbreaks of self-limiting gastroenteritis.
Rotavirus is a reovirus with a double-stranded, segmented RNA genome, and is a major cause in infants, not predominantly adult cruise ship outbreaks.
Adenoviruses types 40/41 cause gastroenteritis but they are DNA viruses, not RNA viruses.
Norovirus (Calicivirus) is the classic 'cruise ship' virus, highly contagious and resistant to environment, causing acute vomiting/diarrhea.

statement: Which of the following describes the unique genomic structure and replication strategy of members of the Reoviridae family?
options: A segmented negative-polarity RNA genome that undergoes cap-snatching in the nucleus
A linear molecule of single-stranded positive-polarity RNA that serves directly as mRNA
Multiple segments of double-stranded RNA requiring a virion-associated polymerase
A double-stranded DNA genome that replicates using a reverse transcriptase intermediate
A single molecule of circular negative-polarity RNA
correctOption: Multiple segments of double-stranded RNA requiring a virion-associated polymerase
optionExplanations: This describes the orthomyxovirus family (influenza), which uses a segmented negative-sense RNA genome and nuclear replication.
This describes the picornavirus or calicivirus families, which have positive-sense ssRNA genomes.

Reoviruses are unique among human pathogens for having a segmented double-stranded RNA genome. Because host cells lack enzymes to transcribe dsRNA, the virus must carry its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the virion.
This describes hepadnaviruses (HBV), which use reverse transcriptase, unlike the RNA-based reoviruses.
This describes certain other RNA viruses like bunyaviruses or arenaviruses, but not reoviruses, which have segmented dsRNA.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 226 (Book Page): The genome of all RNA viruses consists of single-stranded RNA, except for members of the reovirus family, which have a double-stranded RNA genome.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of adenoviruses, papillomaviruses, polyomaviruses, poxviruses, herpesviruses, hepadnaviruses, picornaviruses, hepeviruses, caliciviruses, and reoviruses
statement: During the replicative cycle of Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), what is the specific role of the full-length positive-strand RNA transcript within the host cell cytoplasm?
options: It integrates directly into the host cell DNA to form a stable episome
It binds to the ACE-2 receptor to facilitate viral attachment
It serves as the template for synthesis of the minus-strand DNA genome
It is translated into the HBsAg filaments found in the blood
It functions as a ribozyme to cleave host cell ribosomal RNA
correctOption: It serves as the template for synthesis of the minus-strand DNA genome
optionExplanations: RNA cannot integrate into DNA; it must first be reverse transcribed into DNA. Integration of HBV DNA is not a required step for its replication.
ACE-2 is the receptor for SARS-CoV-2. HBV uses the sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide for entry into hepatocytes.

HBV is a pararetrovirus. In the cytoplasm, the full-length positive-strand RNA (pre-genome) is packaged into the nucleocapsid and used as a template by the viral reverse transcriptase to synthesize the negative-strand DNA of the new genome.
HBsAg filaments are composed of surface protein and are synthesized from smaller, subgenomic mRNAs, not the full-length pre-genome RNA.
The HDV (Hepatitis Delta) genome is a ribozyme, not the HBV pre-genome RNA. HBV does not cleave host rRNA.

The minus strand then serves as the template for the plus strand of the genome DNA.]

statement: When comparing the structural and genomic organization of Orthomyxoviridae and Paramyxoviridae, which diagnostic contrast is most significant for understanding their evolutionary potential for pandemics?
options: Paramyxoviruses possess a segmented genome, allowing for antigenic shift via reassortment.
Only Paramyxoviruses contain a virion-associated RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
Orthomyxoviruses have a positive-polarity genome, while Paramyxoviruses have a negative-polarity genome.
Orthomyxoviruses possess a segmented genome, allowing for antigenic shift via reassortment.
Paramyxoviruses lack an envelope, making them more stable in the environment than Orthomyxoviruses.
correctOption: Orthomyxoviruses possess a segmented genome, allowing for antigenic shift via reassortment.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Paramyxoviruses (e.g., Measles, Mumps) have a non-segmented genome and therefore do not undergo antigenic shift through reassortment.
Incorrect. Both families are negative-sense RNA viruses and must carry their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the virion to synthesize mRNA.
Incorrect. Both Orthomyxoviridae and Paramyxoviridae are negative-polarity, single-stranded RNA viruses.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: Which morphological description accurately characterizes the Rhabdoviridae family, such as the Rabies virus, and the Filoviridae family, such as the Ebola virus?
options: Rhabdoviruses have a segmented genome; Filoviruses have circular RNA.

correctOption: Rhabdoviruses are bullet-shaped; Filoviruses are long, pleomorphic filaments.

Page 348 (Book Page): Ebola virus... Filoviruses are long filamentous (filo = thread) enveloped viruses. They are the longest viruses.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of adenoviruses, papillomaviruses, polyomaviruses, poxviruses, herpesviruses, hepadnaviruses, picornaviruses, hepeviruses, caliciviruses, and reoviruses
statement: In the replication cycle of the hepatitis B virus (HBV), which of the following describes the unique function of the virus-encoded DNA polymerase?

It cleaves the Gag-Pol polyprotein to initiate the synthesis of viral surface antigens.

optionExplanations: The polymerase synthesizes DNA from an RNA template, not RNA from a DNA template (which is the job of cellular RNA polymerase II).
Protease cleaves polyproteins in retroviruses; HBV does not use this mechanism for surface antigen synthesis.
Integration is an obligatory step for retroviruses, but for HBV, while some integration occurs, it is not a required step for replication.
HBV uses host cell RNA polymerase to synthesize mRNA, but the DNA polymerase is viral, not host-derived.

HBV is a hepadnavirus that replicates through an RNA intermediate; the viral polymerase has reverse transcriptase activity that converts RNA into the DNA genome for new virions late in the replication cycle.

Synthesis of the genome takes place within the newly assembled virion nucleocapsid core in the cytoplasm.

statement: A 19-year-old college student presents with severe pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. The laboratory identifies atypical lymphocytes on a blood smear. The surface antigen (HBsAg) for its outer protein coat

HDV possesses its own internal protein, the delta antigen, to coat its RNA genome; it uses the surface antigen (HBsAg), not the core antigen (HBcAg), of HBV for its exterior.
HBV uses reverse transcriptase for its own replication (RNA to DNA), but HDV has an RNA genome and does not use a reverse transcriptase step.

statement: During the replication cycle of the Variola virus, the transcription of viral early messenger RNA occurs in the host cell cytoplasm. Why is this virus family unable to utilize the host cell's DNA-dependent RNA polymerase for this process?

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: The emergence of a 'novel' strain of Influenza A virus, such as the 2009 H1N1 S-OIV, usually results in a pandemic. Which unique conceptual aspect of the Orthomyxoviridae genome allows for the rapid creation of these quadruple-reassortant viruses?

The segmented nature of the RNA genome allowing exchange of genetic pieces
The presence of two copies of the RNA genome (diploid status)
Integration of the viral genome into host DNA as an obligatory step
A circular, single-stranded RNA genome that allows for rolling circle replication
correctOption: The segmented nature of the RNA genome allowing exchange of genetic pieces
optionExplanations: The RNA polymerase of Influenza is actually error-prone (lack of proofreading), which leads to antigenic drift; it is the segmentation that leads to reassortment.

Because the Influenza genome is divided into 8 segments, if two different strains infect the same cell, the progeny can package a mix of segments from both parents (reassortment), leading to a radical new antigenic shift.
Only Retroviruses are diploid; Orthomyxoviruses are haploid with multiple segments.

Note that in reassortment, entire segments of RNA are exchanged, each one of which codes for a single protein. Page 299 (Book Page): S-OIV is a quadruple reassortant: The hemagglutinin, nucleoprotein, and nonstructural protein genes are of North American swine origin...

Adenovirus Type 4
Hepatitis B virus
Human Immunodeficiency Virus
Human Papillomavirus Type 16
correctOption: Hepatitis B virus
optionExplanations: Herpesviruses replicate their DNA using a viral DNA-dependent DNA polymerase via a rolling circle mechanism, not through an RNA intermediate.
Adenoviruses possess a linear double-stranded DNA genome and use a protein-primed mechanism for DNA replication, relying on a DNA-dependent DNA polymerase.

Hepatitis B virus (HBV), a Hepadnavirus, is unique among DNA viruses. After entering the nucleus, its DNA is converted to CCC DNA, which is transcribed into a pregenomic RNA. This RNA is then reverse-transcribed by the viral polymerase into progeny DNA genomes within the cytoplasm.
While HIV uses reverse transcriptase, it produces a DNA intermediate from an RNA genome to integrate into the host; it does not produce its final progeny genome as DNA through this pathway.
Human Papillomavirus utilizes host cell DNA polymerase during the S phase to replicate its circular DNA genome; it does not involve reverse transcription.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 330 (Book Page): [Hepadnaviruses are the only viruses that produce genome DNA by reverse transcription with viral RNA as the template.]

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of adenoviruses, papillomaviruses, polyomaviruses, poxviruses, herpesviruses, hepadnaviruses, picornaviruses, hepeviruses, caliciviruses, and reoviruses
statement: In the classification of enteric viral pathogens, Rotavirus is distinguished by its unique genomic arrangement. How is the genetic material of this virus organized?
options: A single molecule of circular DNA
A single molecule of linear, single-stranded DNA
Eight segments of negative-polarity RNA
Eleven segments of double-stranded RNA
Two identical strands of positive-polarity RNA
correctOption: Eleven segments of double-stranded RNA
optionExplanations: Circular DNA is found in polyomaviruses and papillomaviruses, not reoviruses.
Linear single-stranded DNA is the genomic structure of parvoviruses, such as B19 virus.
Eight segments of negative-polarity RNA are the hallmark of Influenza A and B viruses (Orthomyxoviridae).
Correct. Rotaviruses (members of the Reoviridae family) possess a genome consisting of 11 distinct segments of double-stranded RNA.
Two identical strands of positive RNA (diploid) are characteristic of retroviruses like HIV.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 335 (Book Page): Rotavirus has a segmented, double-stranded RNA genome... The rotavirus genome has 11 segments.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of adenoviruses, papillomaviruses, polyomaviruses, poxviruses, herpesviruses, hepadnaviruses, picornaviruses, hepeviruses, caliciviruses, and reoviruses
statement: Which of the following DNA viruses is unique because it undergoes its entire replicative cycle within the cytoplasm of the host cell?
options: Hepatitis B virus
Herpes simplex virus type 1
Poxvirus
Adenovirus
Human papillomavirus
correctOption: Poxvirus
optionExplanations: Hepadnaviruses like HBV replicate in the nucleus; although they use reverse transcription, the initial template synthesis occurs intranuclearly.
Herpesviruses are enveloped DNA viruses that replicate in the nucleus and notably obtain their envelope by budding from the nuclear membrane.
Poxviruses are the largest DNA viruses and are unique because they carry their own DNA-dependent RNA polymerase within the virion, allowing them to replicate in the cytoplasm instead of the nucleus.
Adenoviruses are nonenveloped DNA viruses that replicate their genome and transcribe mRNA within the nucleus using host machinery.
Human papillomaviruses are small nonenveloped DNA viruses that rely strictly on host nuclear polymerases for replication and transcription.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 214 (Book Page): [DNA viruses, with one exception, replicate in the nucleus and use the host cell DNA-dependent RNA polymerase to synthesize their mRNA. The poxviruses are the exception because they replicate in the cytoplasm, where they do not have access to the host cell RNA polymerase.]

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: A patient presents with acute jaundice and malaise. Serological evaluation for Hepatitis B virus (HBV) reveals that both Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and Hepatitis B surface antibody (HBsAb) are undetectable. Which of the following findings would most accurately confirm a current infection during this 'window phase'?
options: Positive test for HBcAb
Absence of total core antibody
Negative test for HBV DNA polymerase
Positive test for HBeAg
Positive test for HBsAg
correctOption: Positive test for HBcAb
optionExplanations: During the window phase, HBcAb (specifically IgM) is the only reliable marker of recent or current infection because HBsAg has cleared and HBsAb has not yet reached detectable levels.
Total HBcAb is always positive during the window phase; its absence would indicate that the patient has never been infected with HBV.
HBV DNA polymerase is an indicator of viral replication and would typically be positive during active infection, not negative.

While HBeAg is an indicator of high infectivity, its presence or absence does not define the window phase, which is specifically characterized by the gap between HBsAg disappearance and HBsAb appearance.
The window phase is defined by the absence of detectable HBsAg; therefore, a positive HBsAg test would exclude the patient from being in the window phase.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 332 (Book Page): Note that there is a period of several weeks when HBsAg has disappeared but HBsAb is not yet detectable. This is the window phase. At this time, the HBcAb is always positive and can be used to make the diagnosis.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: The Hepatitis Delta Virus (HDV) is termed a 'defective' virus because it lacks the genetic information to synthesize its own outer coat. How does HDV acquire its clinical capability to infect hepatocytes?
options: By encoding a fusion protein that allows direct cell-to-cell spread
By acquiring a lipid bilayer from the nuclear membrane
By utilizing the reverse transcriptase of a Retrovirus
By integrating its circular RNA into the host cell DNA
By using the Hepatitis B surface antigen as its envelope
correctOption: By using the Hepatitis B surface antigen as its envelope
optionExplanations: HDV does not encode a fusion protein for cell-to-cell spread; it relies on the HBsAg-mediated entry mechanism to infect new cells via the blood.
While it is enveloped, HDV cannot form a functional envelope without HBsAg; it doesn't just spontaneously take host nuclear membrane.
HDV does not utilize reverse transcriptase; it is an RNA virus that is replicated by host cell RNA polymerase.
HDV is an RNA virus that replicates in the nucleus but does not integrate into the host DNA; only retroviruses have obligatory integration.
HDV requires the presence of HBV to provide HBsAg, which it uses to package its own RNA and delta antigen to form infectious virions.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 337 (Book Page): HDV is unusual in that it is a defective virus (i.e., it cannot replicate by itself because it does not have the genes for its envelope protein). HDV can replicate only in cells also infected with HBV because HDV uses the surface antigen of HBV (HBsAg) as its envelope protein.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: Which of the following characteristics accurately describes the genome and polarity of the Rubella virus, distinguishing it from members of the Paramyxoviridae family?
options: Circular, negative-polarity RNA
Segmented, negative-polarity RNA
Single-stranded, positive-polarity RNA
Single-stranded, negative-polarity RNA
Double-stranded, segmented RNA
correctOption: Single-stranded, positive-polarity RNA
optionExplanations: Circular, negative-polarity RNA is characteristic of Deltavirus (HDV) or Bunyaviridae.
Segmented, negative-polarity RNA is characteristic of Orthomyxoviridae (Influenza), not Rubella.
Rubella virus, as a togavirus, has a nonsegmented, single-stranded RNA genome with positive polarity.
Single-stranded, negative-polarity RNA is characteristic of Paramyxoviridae (Measles, Mumps) and Rhabdoviridae.
Double-stranded, segmented RNA is characteristic of Reoviridae (Rotavirus).
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 315 (Book Page): Rubella virus is a member of the togavirus family. It is composed of a single-stranded, nonsegmented RNA genome... unlike the paramyxoviruses, such as measles and mumps viruses, it has a positive-strand RNA and therefore has no virion polymerase.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: Which of the following morphological characteristics is unique to the family Retroviridae among all human viral families?
options: The acquisition of the envelope by budding from the plasma membrane.
The presence of two identical copies of the RNA genome (diploid).
The requirement for a virus-encoded RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
The possession of a single-stranded RNA genome of positive polarity.
The presence of a helical nucleocapsid surrounded by an envelope.
correctOption: The presence of two identical copies of the RNA genome (diploid).
optionExplanations: Many enveloped viruses, including Flaviviruses and Paramyxoviruses, bud from the outer cell membrane, making this a common feature.
Retroviridae are the only human viruses that are diploid, meaning they carry two identical molecules of single-stranded RNA.
Negative-strand RNA viruses like Rhabdoviridae carry an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; Retroviridae carry an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase).
Many families, such as Picornaviridae and Flaviviridae, possess positive-polarity single-stranded RNA, thus it is not a unique trait.
Helical nucleocapsids are found in several other families including Orthomyxoviridae and Paramyxoviridae, so this is not unique to Retroviridae.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 218 (Book Page): Almost all viruses contain only a single copy of their genome (i.e., they are haploid). The exception is the retrovirus family, whose members have two copies of their RNA genome (i.e., they are diploid).

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: What is the defining diagnostic criterion that classifies Hepatitis D Virus (HDV) as a 'defective' virus?
options: Its genome consists of DNA that cannot be transcribed without a helper Adenovirus
It lacks a functional RNA polymerase and must use the host cell's DNA polymerase
It requires the presence of Hepatitis B Surface Antigen (HBsAg) to form its outer protein coat
It can only infect individuals who are already deficient in secretory IgA
It undergoes replication exclusively in the gallbladder rather than hepatocytes
correctOption: It requires the presence of Hepatitis B Surface Antigen (HBsAg) to form its outer protein coat
optionExplanations: The HDV genome is single-stranded circular RNA, not DNA.
HDV uses host RNA polymerase II for its replication, but its 'defectiveness' specifically refers to its inability to produce an envelope.
HDV is the only medically important human virus that is defective by needing a specific helper virus (HBV) to provide its envelope (HBsAg) for virion assembly.
HDV infection depends on HBV status (co-infection or superinfection), not on the host's IgA levels.
HDV replicates in the nucleus of hepatocytes, similar to other hepatitis viruses, but its clinical significance is liver-based, not gallbladder-based.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 337 (Book Page): HDV is unusual in that it is a defective virus (i.e., it cannot replicate by itself because it does not have the genes for its envelope protein). HDV can replicate only in cells also infected with HBV because HDV uses the surface antigen of HBV (HBsAg) as its envelope protein.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of adenoviruses, papillomaviruses, polyomaviruses, poxviruses, herpesviruses, hepadnaviruses, picornaviruses, hepeviruses, caliciviruses, and reoviruses
statement: A patient presents with symptoms of hepatitis. Laboratory results show that Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) has recently disappeared and Hepatitis B surface antibody (HBsAb) is not yet detectable. In this 'window phase,' which marker is essential for confirming an acute infection?
options: Detection of high levels of Hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) in the serum.
Presence of circulating Dane particles visualized by electron microscopy.
Detection of IgM antibody against the Hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAb).
Identification of HBx protein integrated into the host cell DNA.
Observation of anti-HBs IgG indicating successful immune resolution.
correctOption: Detection of IgM antibody against the Hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAb).
optionExplanations: HBeAg is a marker of high infectivity and active replication, but it often disappears before the HBsAg window phase concludes.
Dane particles (complete virions) are generally not found in the blood once HBsAg has been cleared from the circulation.
During the window phase, IgM HBcAb is the only detectable marker of a recent acute infection, as HBsAg and HBsAb are absent or complexed.
The HBx protein is associated with oncogenesis in chronic carriers and is not a routine diagnostic marker for acute infection stages.
Anti-HBs IgG marks the end of the window phase and signifies immunity; its absence is what defines the 'window' itself.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 332 (Book Page): Note that there is a period of several weeks when HBsAg has disappeared but HBsAb is not yet detectable. This is the window phase. At this time, the HBcAb is always positive and can be used to make the diagnosis.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: Which statement accurately describes the requirement for the replication of Hepatitis Delta Virus (HDV)?
options: It requires integration into the hepatocyte chromosome to function
It requires host cell reverse transcriptase to synthesize its DNA
It requires a helper virus to provide its RNA-dependent RNA polymerase
It requires the presence of Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) as its outer coat
It requires a co-infection with Hepatitis A to enter the cell
correctOption: It requires the presence of Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) as its outer coat
optionExplanations: HDV does not integrate into host chromosomes; it replicates as a ribozyme in the nucleus.
HDV uses host cell RNA polymerase, not reverse transcriptase, to replicate its circular RNA genome.
HDV carries its own single protein (delta antigen) but its replication is mediated by the host, not a helper virus polymerase.
HDV is a defective virus that cannot produce its own envelope; it must 'borrow' HBsAg from a co-infecting Hepatitis B virus to form infectious progeny.
HDV is exclusively associated with HBV; Hepatitis A (a Picornavirus) has no relationship with the replication or entry of HDV.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 337 (Book Page): HDV can replicate only in cells also infected with HBV because HDV uses the surface antigen of HBV (HBsAg) as its envelope protein. HBV is therefore the helper virus for HDV.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: Which of the following descriptions accurately characterizes the unique pleomorphic morphology of the Filoviridae family, which includes the Ebola and Marburg viruses?
options: Brick-shaped complex particles with a disk-shaped core
Bullet-shaped virions with a single-layered lipid envelope
Spherical particles with a corona of club-shaped spikes
Highly elongated, thread-like filaments that may be thousands of nanometers long
Small, non-enveloped icosahedral capsids containing circular DNA
correctOption: Highly elongated, thread-like filaments that may be thousands of nanometers long
optionExplanations: This describes Poxviruses (e.g., Variola virus).
This describes Rhabdoviruses (e.g., Rabies).
This describes Coronaviruses (Coronaviridae).
Filoviruses (from the Latin 'filum' for thread) are distinct for their extremely long, pleomorphic, filamentous shape, which can sometimes appear like a 'shepherd's crook'.
This describes Papillomaviruses (e.g., HPV).
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 245 (Book Page): Filoviruses... They are highly pleomorphic, long filaments that are 80 nm in diameter but can be thousands of nanometers long. The term filo means “thread” and refers to the long filaments. Page 348 (Book Page): Filoviruses are long filamentous (filo = thread) enveloped viruses. They are the longest viruses, often measuring thousands of nanometers.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of adenoviruses, papillomaviruses, polyomaviruses, poxviruses, herpesviruses, hepadnaviruses, picornaviruses, hepeviruses, caliciviruses, and reoviruses
statement: Which of the following descriptions accurately characterizes the genome of Picornaviruses, such as poliovirus and hepatitis A virus?
options: Double-stranded, circular, supercoiled DNA.
Single-stranded, linear, nonsegmented RNA with positive polarity.
Single-stranded, circular DNA with negative polarity.
Single-stranded, segmented RNA with negative polarity.
Double-stranded, linear RNA segments with negative polarity.
correctOption: Single-stranded, linear, nonsegmented RNA with positive polarity.
optionExplanations: This describes Papillomaviruses and Polyomaviruses, which are DNA viruses, not Picornaviruses.
Picornaviruses are small, nonenveloped viruses containing a single-stranded, nonsegmented, positive-polarity RNA genome that functions directly as mRNA.
This description does not match any major human virus; Parvoviruses are single-stranded but linear DNA.
This describes Orthomyxoviruses like influenza, which have segmented negative-polarity RNA.
This describes Reoviruses, which have double-stranded RNA, not Picornaviruses.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 245 (Book Page): [Picornaviruses... have single-stranded, linear, nonsegmented, positive-polarity RNA within a naked icosahedral capsid.]

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: When comparing the structural and replicative characteristics of Orthomyxoviruses and Paramyxoviruses, which feature serves as the primary distinction between these two families?
options: The segmentation of the RNA genome
The polarity of the single-stranded RNA genome
The presence of a lipid lipoprotein envelope
The requirement for a virion-associated RNA polymerase
The symmetry of the viral nucleocapsid
correctOption: The segmentation of the RNA genome
optionExplanations: Orthomyxoviruses (e.g., Influenza) have segmented genomes (typically 8 segments), while Paramyxoviruses (e.g., Measles, Mumps) have a single nonsegmented RNA strand.
Both Orthomyxoviruses and Paramyxoviruses possess a negative-polarity single-stranded RNA genome.
Both families are enveloped viruses; the presence of an envelope does not distinguish them from each other.
Both families require an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the virion because their genomes are negative-polarity RNA.
Both families exhibit helical symmetry in their nucleocapsids, making this a similarity rather than a distinction.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 293 (Book Page): The orthomyxoviruses differ from the paramyxoviruses primarily in that the former have a segmented RNA genome (usually eight pieces), whereas the RNA genome of the latter consists of a single piece.

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of adenoviruses, papillomaviruses, polyomaviruses, poxviruses, herpesviruses, hepadnaviruses, picornaviruses, hepeviruses, caliciviruses, and reoviruses
statement: A 10-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with severe watery diarrhea and vomiting for two days. Dehydration is evident. Stool analysis is positive for Rotavirus antigen. Which of the following structural features is characteristic of the viral genome of this causative agent?
options: Double-stranded RNA with 11 segments and no envelope
Single-stranded, positive-polarity RNA with 8 segments
Single-stranded, nonsegmented DNA with an icosahedral capsid
Single-stranded, negative-polarity RNA with a helical nucleocapsid
Circular, double-stranded DNA integrated into the host chromosome
correctOption: Double-stranded RNA with 11 segments and no envelope
optionExplanations: Rotavirus is a Reovirus. Its genome is unique for being double-stranded RNA and segmented into 11 pieces, which allows for genetic reassortment.
Influenza A has 8 segments, but they are negative-polarity RNA. Rotavirus has 11 segments of double-stranded RNA.
This describes Parvovirus B19. Rotavirus is an RNA virus with a double-layered capsid.
This describes Paramyxoviruses or Rhabdoviruses. Rotavirus is nonenveloped and has icosahedral symmetry.
This describes the integrated form of HPV or HBV. Rotavirus does not integrate into host DNA.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 321 (Book Page): [Rotavirus has a segmented, double-stranded RNA genome surrounded by a double-layered icosahedral capsid without an envelope. The rotavirus genome has 11 segments.]

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: A victim of a stray dog bite begins to show signs of agitation and hydrophobia. The virus travels from the site of inoculation in the muscle tissue to the central nervous system. Which physiological pathway is utilized by the Rhabdoviridae family to reach the hippocampal neurons?
options: Retrograde axonal transport within sensory or motor neurons
Passage across the blood-brain barrier via infected macrophages (Trojan horse)
Hematogenous spread via the portal vein during primary viremia
Direct ascending infection via the olfactory nerve following inhalation of aerosols
Movement through the lymphatic vessels to the thoracic duct
correctOption: Retrograde axonal transport within sensory or motor neurons
optionExplanations: Rabies virus uses retrograde axonal transport. This allows it to move from the peripheral site of the bite up the axon to the cell body in the CNS while remaining hidden from immune surveillance.
The 'Trojan horse' mechanism via macrophages is common for HIV, but not for the neurotropic Rhabdoviridae.
Rabies does not have a viremic stage; its spread is strictly neural. Hematogenous spread is typical for Polio or Hepatitis viruses.
While aerosol transmission of Rabies can occur in bat caves, the standard physiological progression from a bite involves axonal transport from the local tissue, not primarily the olfactory route.
Lymphatic spread is common for many viruses but is not the mechanism Rabies uses to bypass the immune system and enter the CNS.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 347 (Book Page): The virus multiplies locally at the bite site, infects the sensory neurons, and moves by axonal transport to the central nervous system. During its transport within the nerve, the virus is sheltered from the immune system and little, if any, immune response occurs. The virus multiplies in the central nervous system and then travels down the peripheral nerves to the salivary glands...

category: Explain the morphological, pathological, and diagnostic aspects of retroviruses, flaviviruses, togaviruses, coronaviruses, deltaviruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, orthomyxoviruses, and filoviruses
statement: Regarding the Togavirus family, specifically Rubella virus, which statement regarding its genome and transmission is correct?
options: It has a negative-polarity RNA genome and is transmitted via the fecal-oral route
It has a double-stranded DNA genome and is transmitted by respiratory droplets
It has a segmented RNA genome and is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes
It has a positive-polarity RNA genome and is transmitted transplacentally
It has a diploid RNA genome and is transmitted by blood transfusions
correctOption: It has a positive-polarity RNA genome and is transmitted transplacentally
optionExplanations: Rubella has positive-polarity RNA, not negative, and is not an enterovirus; it does not use the fecal-oral route.
Togaviruses are RNA viruses, not DNA viruses.
While some Togaviruses (Alphaviruses) are segmented or mosquito-borne, Rubella is a Rubivirus, which is non-segmented and human-to-human only.
Rubella is a Togavirus with a non-segmented positive-polarity RNA genome. It is unique among the childhood exanthems for its significant risk of transplacental transmission and teratogenicity.
Retroviruses are diploid; Togaviruses are haploid.
citation: In book "Levinson's Review of Medical Microbiology & Immunology", Page 315 (Book Page): Rubella virus ... has a positive-strand RNA and therefore has no virion polymerase. ... The virus is transmitted via respiratory droplets and from mother to fetus transplacentally.
